'Freakish' discovery of 9 million-year-old capybara tooth supports idea that Atacama wasn't always a desert
->Live Science | More on "Ancient Atacama Desert climate history" at BigEarthData.ai

external.description: Researchers have discovered a roughly 9 million year old tooth belonging to a large, water-loving relative of modern day capybaras in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. The fossilized molar adds to previous evidence suggesting that it's unlikely the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, was continuously dry for the last 40 million years. The Atacama Desert, possibly the oldest desert on Earth, takes up the northern third of Chile. It's bounded by the Chilean Coast Range to the west, which blocks rain from the Pacific Ocean, and the enormous Andes to the east, which obstruct rain from the Atlantic Ocean. The driest part of the desert's hyperarid region gets less than 0.08 inches (2 mm) of rainfall a month. Recent research estimates the Atacama's hyperarid core started forming between 47.8 million and 33.9 million years ago, in the Mid- to Late-Eocene, 20 million years before the Andes formed. It suggests the mountain ranges weren't the cause for the desert's aridification, and may have only intensified it. external.description: Newswise — Could artificial intelligence (AI) help identify an Ebola vaccine target, predict severe weather or write code for a supercomputer? Each summer, Argonne welcomes hundreds of undergraduate and graduate student interns to gain hands-on experience in research, technology development and lab operations. This year several worked on projects focused on using AI to accelerate scientific discovery. Their work is helping shape the future of AI-enabled biomedicine, weather forecasting and high performance computing (HPC). Here are the stories from four of these early-career researchers. Shreya Ganesh Shreya Ganesh, a senior in data science at Purdue University, served on a team working to understand how to create a vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola. A screenshot of a headline to a Guardian column by Adrian Chiles. It reads 'My latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit - and the benefits are myriad'

(Alt-text for next image)
I was carrying out maintenance on the hull when the ion drive exploded. The force of the blast sent me hurtling away from the body of the craft, where I could only watch helplessly as it ruptured and burst, section by section, expelling the rest of the crew into space. While I was kept anchored to a large segment of the living quarters by my tether, my crewmates -  my friends - went sailing on by me, already suffocated by the airless void, scattershot corpses heading for oblivion.
That was six months ago. My life since has been amongst the debris. With all long-range comms disabled or destroyed, I am adrift, lost. But not alone.
In the first weeks after my shipwrecking, I became aware of another creature living amidst the remnants. I don’t know its name or provenance, but I suspect it is some kind of space-borne parasite. My first glimpse of it came as I was scavenging in the lower decks. Turning a corner, I found the body of an engineer, splayed out on the floor, its chest pulsating, so at first I thought him alive. Then I saw it - a large shape, near-transparent, a thin proboscis lodged in between the engineer’s ribs, sucking on his flesh. As it sucked, the human’s body seemed to deflate, while at the same time the creature’s transparency began to colour pink.
(Continued on next alt-text)

(Continued from previous alt-text)
Since then, I have come across countless other bodies, some stripped of flesh, some of bone, some of skin. And the creature I have seen many times too - each time pinker, bloodier, as though building itself layer by layer into completeness.
I believe that the creature’s survival depends on its ability to adapt to its circumstances, to create itself anew from its surroundings. Gradually it is becoming bigger, stronger, smarter.
Weaponless, stranded, I am helpless to defend myself against it.
Unless by doing what it does.
For months I have been collecting the creature’s excretions and using them as fertilizer in the improvised greenhouse I have erected in the ship’s sauna. The only plants I was able to scavenge from the ship’s garden were a handful of established kiwi fruit vines and these I have nurtured as though they were my own children.
A week ago I carried out my first harvest - a bowl of mature fruits, bred on the waste from the creature. These I devoured, from seed to skin - the skin, I soon discovered, being the repository of the most useful nutrients - savouring the sweet taste of fresh food after so long living on dried rations.
The results have been promising. I no longer need to use my suit when travelling between the broken parts of the ship; breathing has become optional. Even better, I have found that by ingesting small fragments of the debris through my newly-grown proboscis, I have been able to develop a new skin made of that same metal.
Like the creature I am becoming what I need to be in order to survive.
And if I fear that my humanity is drifting away like the corpses of my friends, into oblivion? That is just the price I have to pay for survival.]

value.text: I will not accept any other future for the Ohio Democratic party that isn't the next Democratic president purging the leadership and forcing them to undergo public humiliation rituals.

Today, I resigned as Vice Chair of the ODP Pride Caucus.
The state party expects us to be a sales team, censoring our voices when we beg candidates not to trade on trans lives. I am still a Democrat, but I will not value party approval over true, defiant advocacy.

Full text below. 👇

images.alt: Part 1 of an open letter of resignation by Arienne Childrey, stepping down as Vice Chair and member of the Ohio Democratic Party (ODP) Pride Caucus. She states that party leadership treats the caucus as a recruitment and sales team rather than a representative body. She cites an incident where the ODP censored and denied permission for the caucus to post a letter by two trans leaders addressing harmful comments made by Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton. The State Party Chair reportedly called the letter an "unwelcome distraction," which Childrey notes demonstrates how little party leadership values the voices and dignity of LGBTQ+ Democrats.

Since that decision, every Caucus plan, every potential post, and every path forward has been filtered through a lens of strict compliance and ODP approval. That may very well be the party's rule, but following those rules right now is a dereliction of our duty to the LGBTQ+ community.

For me, any rule that silences advocacy for the trans community during this time is an unjust rule, and I see no obligation to follow it. In alignment with the words of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. in his Letter from Birmingham Jail:

“One has not only a legal but a moral responsibility to obey just laws. Conversely, one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws.”

We are living in incredibly dangerous times for the trans community. We are in an era where the GOP has so thoroughly weaponized trans lives that even some formerly self-professing allies within our own party have fallen prey to the rhetoric. Looking at the national trend towards Democratic anti-trans triangulation, as well as our own internal conversations, it is clear to me that this shift is much more than a simple coincidence.

We have to speak up—loudly, strongly, and unapologetically—or I fear what our 2028 choices may look like. The ODP would like everyone to believe they are a "big tent" party. However, their successful efforts to silence even the Pride Caucus—even in cases where we are simply begging our candidates not to trade on our lives for perceived electoral advantage—has proven otherwise. The tent hasn't gotten any bigger; it has simply shifted, leaving many trans individuals, progressives, and allies out in the rain.

I will continue to advocate, organize, and fight for our community with everything I have. But I can no longer compromise my own moral principles by remaining part of a caucus that appears more interested in party approval than in true, defiant advocacy.

Sincerely,
Arienne Childrey
